implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the GoF shape visible in the type system: declare an interface for the component, then a class that implements it, stores the inner value and forwards every member, so a missing pass-through is a compile error rather than a silent behaviour change. Stacking is ordinary composition - new LoggingSource(new RetryingSource(http, 3)) - and the decorator order is the nesting order. This is the right default for object contracts with one or more methods; the @decorator syntax that TypeScript 5.0 made standard is a different mechanism (it customises class declarations and members at definition time and cannot wrap an object instance), so object decoration stays plain composition.

variants.name: Class implementing the component interface and delegating
variants.idiom_name: class (or abstract base decorator) that implements the interface, stores the inner value and forwards; the compiler enforces the forwarding obligation

pitfalls: Composition order decides behaviour: a retry wrapping a cache differs from a cache wrapping a retry, and the type system cannot express which order was intended - fix the order in one factory function.
Wrapping breaks `this` for methods borrowed from the inner object (const f = inner.load) and hides private #fields; bind or call through the wrapper.
The compiler checks signatures, not behaviour: a decorator can satisfy the interface and still break the contract (swallow errors, return undefined) - Liskov has to be tested, not compiled.

variants.name: Typed higher-order function wrapper
variants.idiom_name: function taking the inner function and returning a wrapped one with the same type, using generics/variadic tuple types to preserve arguments and results
variants.implementation_notes: For single-operation contracts the typed higher-order function is leaner than any class: `logCall<Args extends unknown[], R>(fn: (...args: Args) => R)` returns a wrapper that logs and forwards while keeping the exact argument and return types, and composition is nesting - withLogging(withRetry(fetchJson, 3)). TypeScript's utility types (ThisParameterType, OmitThisParameter, variadic tuple types) exist to keep `this` and argument shapes intact, which is the price of the functional form. It is also the only option for standalone functions, because decorator syntax applies to class members only; when the contract has several methods, the class variant avoids threading each method through functions.
pitfalls: Methods need extra typing to survive wrapping - this-typed signatures require ThisParameterType/OmitThisParameter, otherwise the wrapper is callable but no longer type-checks as the method it wraps.
Stack traces and function names change (jsmanifest/TypeScript-focused guides document migrating between wrapper styles): if call-site attribution matters, copy name and metadata explicitly.
Wrappers that use `any`/`as` casts to stay generic silently widen the type, so the composed function no longer matches the interface it is assigned to - annotate the wrapped type explicitly.
